title: Geordie Shore star and illegal finfluencer sentenced for promoting high-risk investments on social media
raw_summary: Aaron Chalmers, a reality TV star and social media content creator, and finfluencer Jason Agbodza have been sentenced for illegally promoting an unauthorised foreign exchange trading scheme on social media. Chalmers, 39 and from Newcastle, was sentenced at City of London Magistrates Court. He previously pleaded guilty and today (19 November) was fined £3,072 and ordered to pay costs of £2,836.Having risen to fame on Geordie Shore, Chalmers has more than 2 million followers on Instagram. Agbodza, 35, of London, was also fined £1,173 and ordered to pay costs of £2,114 after pleading guilty.Both men encouraged followers to invest in foreign exchange (forex or FX) trading through contracts for difference (CFDs), without being authorised to promote them. CFDs are high-risk derivatives, and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has previously found that approximately 80% of customers lose money when investing in them.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said:'With more than two million Instagram followers, Chalmers exploited his online influence to illegally promote investments to a vast audience. Agbodza made significant profits from an unlawful investment scheme. These cases send a clear message: we will take decisive action against those that break the law and put consumers at risk.'Separately, earlier this year the FCA issued cautions to 2 individuals for posting illegal financial promotions on social media. The cautions will appear on their criminal records.The FCA is also calling on social media platforms to do more to stop illegal financial promotions at source. Google, Bing (Microsoft), Meta, X and TikTok have agreed to restrict paid-for financial services advertising to FCA-authorised firms, helping to reduce scam adverts significantly. But illegal promotions remain prevalent. During the FCA's international week of action on unlawful finfluencers, 66% of illegal financial adverts identified on social media were linked to firms or individuals already on the FCA Warning List. Platforms need to monitor more closely and intervene faster.Notes to editorsAaron Chalmers' date of birth is 26/05/1987. He pleaded guilty to illegal promotions on social media on 22 April 2026 at Westminster Magistrates' Court.Aaron Chalmers’ costs to pay consist of a victim surcharge of £1,229 and court costs of £1,607.Jason Agbodza's date of birth is 13/07/1990. He was sentenced at City of London Magistrates Court.Jason Agbodza’s costs to pay consist of a statutory surcharge of £1,645 and court costs of £469.Making unauthorised financial promotions is an offence under Sections 21 and 25 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, punishable upon conviction by a fine and/or up to 2 years of imprisonment.In the UK, the FCA has imposed restrictions on how CFDs and CFD-like options can be sold and marketed to retail customers. The FCA has been carrying out work to address consumer harm in the UK in this sector.In April 2026, the FCA led an international week of action against unlawful finfluencers. It identified 1,267 illegal financial adverts, which reached a minimum of 2,338,372 UK accounts. 66% of these adverts were from firms or individuals already on the FCA Warning List. The data on illegal adverts, UK account reach and Warning List matches was specific to Meta platforms.Consumers can use the FCA's Firm Checker to see whether a firm is authorised and has permission to offer the service it is promoting.The FCA's InvestSmart website provides information to help people understand investment risks and make better informed decisions.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

title: The courage to change
raw_summary: Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at TheCityUK National Conference 2026. Our willingness to do things differently in this country has helped make our financial services sector one of the most innovative in the world.We didn’t get here by accident.It took ambitious firms, given the right amount of room to experiment.The FCA recognised the importance of pushing the boundaries with Project Innovate in 2014.And the world’s first Regulatory Sandbox in 2016, allowing firms to test innovative ideas with dedicated FCA support.By 2024, fintech was the most significant job source in UK financial services.Fintech firms contribute positively to growth, productivity and infrastructure.No wonder the UK is Europe’s top spot for fintech investment.But we can’t take that position for granted.Investment is down. Global competition is up. Funding is getting harder to come by.And operational disruption is no longer a matter of if, but when.We’ve recently seen the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange robbed of more than $6 billion.And a global tech outage that left millions of employees without the tools they need to do their jobs.Market integrity risks have never been greater.That's not a reason to hold back on innovation.If anything, it’s a reason to keep going. We can’t solve these challenges if we stand still.But we need to be clear-eyed along the way.That doesn’t mean certain.None of us can wait for perfect information.You decide whether to build, hire or invest before knowing if the idea will work.We often need to decide whether to act – and how – without the full picture.Uncertainty comes with the territory.And in a rapidly changing world, we need to be comfortable making decisions in the face of it.The decisions that got us here were made that way. The ones ahead will be too.

title: Insurance firms called on to improve claims handling
raw_summary: The FCA and Financial Ombudsman Service have published a report setting out what insurers need to focus on to ensure claims are dealt with promptly, clearly and fairly. We are helping firms learn from Financial Ombudsman complaints and strengthen their claims handling in line with our existing rules to improve service quality for insurance customers.The report highlights where claims handling can improve and explains the key rules firms need to meet.Building on findings in our 2025 review of home and travel insurance, it calls on insurers to:Keep claims moving.Give customers clear and timely updates.Take responsibility when problems arise with third parties working on their behalf.While 79% of people who make a claim are satisfied with claims handling (PDF), improvements are needed in consumer understanding and service quality.Chris Knight, director for insurance at the FCA, said: 'Most insurance customers receive a good service, but we know there is room for improvement – and when standards fall short, firms must put things right. These insights will help firms understand our requirements so that claims are handled promptly, clearly and fairly.'The report comes ahead of proposed legislative changes which would require regular joint thematic reports from the Financial Ombudsman and the FCA to help firms learn lessons from complaints handling. It forms part of wider reforms to modernise the redress system to provide greater predictability, certainty and transparency for firms and consumers.Raising insurance standards We have been working to improve standards across insurance markets, expanding this work further following the Which? super-complaint in September 2025.Key actions include:Using our enforcement powers to open 6 insurance Consumer Duty investigations, including 3 involving potential poor claims handling and fair value failures in home and travel insurance.An ongoing premium finance fair value review that has reduced monthly insurance costs. In February, we estimated this was saving consumers around £157m a year.Securing more than £200m in compensation for motor customers with written-off or stolen vehicles.Delivering annual savings of £70m through our GAP insurance intervention following concerns over fair value.More information:Read the joint press release and thematic report on insurance claims handling.We will publish an update by the end of this year on progress against the commitments in our December 2025 response to Which?’s super-complaint.

title: FCA launches world-first platform giving firms new insight into AI innovation
raw_summary: New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities. The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services.Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing.Developed in partnership with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and technology partner NayaOne, the Observatory helps meet the growing demand for greater visibility of AI adoption across the sector.The resource highlights a range of AI use cases shaping financial services, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI.By widening access to market intelligence, the Observatory will help firms of all sizes learn from developments across the market, better understand emerging technologies and make more informed decisions about adopting AI responsibly.Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'AI is creating significant opportunities across financial services, and we’re committed to helping firms understand how the technology is being used.'The AI Spotlight Observatory provides an open and accessible resource that brings together real-world examples of AI adoption, helping firms, innovators and researchers learn from developments across the sector and identify new opportunities for innovation and growth.'Notes to editorsThe FCA’s AI Spotlight Observatory is the first resource of its kind for a regulator globally. It builds on the FCA’s AI Spotlight Digital Showcase, a repository of practical AI solutions across specific themes, by adding new features and capabilities, such as a common taxonomy for comparison, a distinction between use cases and implementations, and the ability to identify emerging patterns across the market.The platform is open and accessible to all users. Registration is required to access more detailed insights, such as target client information, and to request demonstrations directly from innovators featured on the platform.The Observatory will continue to evolve through the addition of new use cases. Firms can apply to be showcased on the platform.CFTE has supported the development of the Observatory across three main areas: creating the taxonomy, building the repository, and socialising the Observatory with the market.The Observatory forms part of CFTE’s wider collaboration with the FCA on AI capability, industry engagement and market intelligence. Alongside initiatives such as the Agentic Academy, CFTE supports the FCA in helping the financial-services sector better understand, structure and respond to the opportunities and challenges created by AI.NayaOne has been responsible for the design and development of the Observatory platform, including the user interface, navigation, search and filtering capabilities.The platform builds on the FCA’s wider work on AI, including itsAI Discussion Paper, AI Sprint, and AI Lab, which includes AI Live Testing and its groundbreaking Supercharged Sandbox supported by NVIDIA, NayaOne and Anthropic.Last month, the FCA published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services.

title: UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise
raw_summary: UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast-evolving threat environment.It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers.Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said: ‘Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance.‘Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.’Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said:‘Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.’Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said:‘We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents.‘The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.’Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risksSeparately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing. The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions. These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area.Notes to editorsThe FCA, PRA and the Bank have jointly published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management.The consultation closes on 26 February 2027.Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year.The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements. The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve.The proposed guidance key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas include:Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management, with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance.Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk, maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts.Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats, applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains.Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly, through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks.Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively, with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned.The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future.A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years.In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI.

title: Helping more people break the cycle of persistent credit card debt
raw_summary: Credit cards are a useful financial tool for many – offering flexibility and helping people manage spending and cash flow.But if customers only make low repayments over a long period, they can end up in debt for years while racking up interest and charges.The persistent debt rules we introduced in 2018 aimed to tackle this.They said that lenders had to identify customers who, over an 18-month period, paid more in interest, fees and charges than towards their balance.Lenders had to contact these customers and encourage them to increase repayments if they could afford it, and if they were still struggling, lenders had to take additional steps to help them repay their balances sustainably.What changed for consumersOur evaluation shows that consumer outcomes improved between 2018 and early 2023. Percentage of accounts in persistent debt

title: FCA charges individual with money laundering
raw_summary: The FCA has charged Raymond Fieldhouse with a money laundering offence. Mr Fieldhouse is accused of laundering over £1.42m made from investment scams between 1 June 2017 and 1 August 2018.Mr Fieldhouse appeared at Stockport Magistrates’ Court on 17 November 2026 where he did not enter a plea. He was remanded in custody until his plea and trial preparation hearing on 22 December 2026 at Southwark Crown Court.Notes to editorsRaymond Fieldhouse was born on 29 April 1982. His nationality is British/Venezuelan. Mr Fieldhouse is accused of money laundering, contrary to section 327 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

title: Getting the full picture of trading in UK shares
raw_summary: Why a complete picture mattersIn today’s market, firms can choose where and how they trade.Previous analysis has found that this competitive landscape benefits firms in wholesale markets. However, trading in UK shares has become more dispersed across venues and different ways of executing trades. Better information about market-wide activity helps firms assess liquidity, make investment decisions and understand trading costs. However, obtaining a complete picture of that activity has become more difficult.As we set out in CP26/30, overall trading activity in UK equity markets has been robust over recent years (see figure 1).

title: What we’re learning from firms engaging with our innovation services
raw_summary: Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion.As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment.Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions.In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.Applications at a glance37% involved AI (up from 31% in 2025), making it the most common technology theme.92% of the firms engaging with our services were doing so for the first time, highlighting continued demand from new innovators.64% of proposed solutions included a retail element, showing continued focus on consumer-facing innovation.The growing use of AIFirms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.Innovation is becoming more interconnectedInnovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.Financial inclusionFirms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over timeWe are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.Looking aheadApplications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
raw_summary: Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected. The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. Providers and Independent Governance Committees would need access to the information necessary to assess whether performance-linked fees offer value for money.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said: 'People's pension savings should work hard for them. We want providers to have greater choice over how they invest for the long term where this can deliver better outcomes for savers.'But greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Any higher charges must be justified by additional value, with firms carefully weighing returns, risks and costs when deciding what is in savers' best interests.'The proposals would bring FCA rules more closely into line with the regime for trust-based pension schemes, where certain performance-linked fees have been excluded from the charge cap since 2023.Greater alignment would support competition and choice and reduce unnecessary complexity for providers operating across both parts of the market.The proposals would give providers an option, not an obligation, to use the exemption. Providers should do so only where it is in savers' interests, and they can meet the relevant protections.The FCA is seeking responses by 14 January 2027 and currently expects to make final rules in summer 2027 following consideration of feedback.Notes to editorsThe consultation is open until Thursday 14 January 2027. Read CP26/40: Exempting performance fees from the workplace pensions charge cap.This work is a priority under the FCA's Pensions Regulatory Priorities (PDF) and forms part of the wider pensions reform.In 2023, the Government changed the rules so certain performance fees sit outside the limit on charges, with protections for members. The proposals build on changes made for trust-based schemes in 2023, while reflecting developments in private markets and strengthening protections in areas such as how investments are valued.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA .

title: Man sentenced over £154m fake takeover bid targeting UK-listed company
raw_summary: Christopher Woolcott has today been given a 2-year prison sentence, suspended for 2 years, after staging a £154m fake takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration Inc. He was also ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and to pay costs of £4,627.73.Mr Woolcott built a sizeable stake in Touchstone, an oil and gas listed company. He then launched a bogus bid to drive up its share price. To give the bid credibility, Mr Woolcott invented several identities, forged takeover documents using Chat GPT and met Touchstone’s chief executive at a central London hotel under a false name. Touchstone ultimately determined that the bid was not legitimate.Had his plan succeeded, he stood to gain as much as £70,000 through the sale of his shares.The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) used a combination of its transaction reporting data, phone records, receipts, CCTV footage and evidence seized to identify Mr Woolcott as the person behind the fraud.Investigators traced three phone numbers used by different supposed individuals to contact Touchstone, to the same handset, and combined voter-register, open source research and FCA trading data to narrow down potential suspects. A parking payment also placed Mr Woolcott’s car near a Ryman store where the forged documents were sent from.Searches of Mr Woolcott's home and workplace later recovered the mobile phone linked to the fabricated identities, including a purported private equity partner, his supposed colleague and a fictitious solicitor.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'Mr Woolcott's fake takeover bid was a calculated attempt to profit by manipulating the market.'Our investigators followed an extensive evidence trail, exposed the fraud and identified the person behind the ruse.‘Anyone tempted to manipulate our markets should know that we are fully committed to identifying, investigating and taking action against those who seek to break the law.'In sentencing, Judge Karu said Mr Woolcott’s operation was deliberate, sophisticated, and planned in which four false identities and forged documents were used to hoodwink Touchstone Exploration Inc with a false takeover bid.Mr Woolcott pleaded guilty on 10 September 2026 to 1 count of fraud by false representation and 3 counts of making a false instrument.The investigation demonstrates how the FCA uses its full range of enforcement powers to disrupt financial crime and protect market integrity.The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025, formally charged Mr Woolcott 16 months later and secured guilty pleas within 18 months of launching the case.Notes to editorsChristopher Woolcott, of Greenwich, London, was born on 23 April 1982.On 10 September 2026, Woolcott pleaded guilty at Westminster Magistrates’ Court to:1 count of fraud by false representation, contrary to sections 1 and 2 of the Fraud Act 2006; and3 counts of making a false instrument, contrary to sections 1 and 6 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981. Fraud by false representation is punishable by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.Making a false instrument is punishable on indictment by a fine and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment.On 10 November 2026 at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Woolcott was sentenced to:a 2 year sentence, suspended for 2 years, and ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work and pay costs of £4627.73; anda 14 months custodial sentence for each of the three forgery offences, to run concurrently with the two year suspended sentence.The FCA opened its criminal investigation in March 2025.Touchstone Exploration Inc is listed on AIM and the Toronto Stock Exchange. It was not under investigation by the FCA in connection with this case.Read the previous FCA press release: Man pleads guilty to fraud and forgery offences relating to fake takeover approach.Tackling market abuse and financial crime is a priority under the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

title: The not-so-fine print: making consumer contracts fair
raw_summary: How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders. When we take action We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use. Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to: Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; andIn some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA. Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress. Examples of cases we've tackledA crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.What we expect of firmsFirms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice. In practice, that means:Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to. Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to usConcerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

title: FCA acts to protect consumers facing demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
raw_summary: We've intervened and Ethica Resolve Limited (Ethica), an FCA authorised firm that services and collects debt on behalf of creditors, has agreed to restrictions. These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Ethica is acting on behalf of West 28th Street Limited (West 28), which bought disguised remuneration loans from a third party. West 28 is not authorised or regulated by the FCA.Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’. However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court. The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved. Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

title: Looking back to move forward: why reviewing our rules matters
raw_summary: Markets evolve. Consumer behaviour changes. Technology creates new opportunities and risks. Rules that were appropriate when they were introduced may need to be updated, simplified or, in some cases, removed altogether.That is why the FCA regularly reviews its rules.

title: FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime
raw_summary: A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing. The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.Notes to editorsRead more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Act now to be resilient in the quantum future
raw_summary: Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.What firms need to do nowSo, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to:Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.How we are supporting firmsWe are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.You can find more information:NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptographyG7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sectorCMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: New FCA rules bring ESG rating providers into UK regulation for the first time
raw_summary: New UK rules for environmental, social and governance (ESG) rating providers will raise standards in the market, helping investors to make better informed decisions. The new framework brings ESG rating providers into FCA regulation for the first time, covering a market that plays an important role in investment decisions. The rules are designed to improve the transparency, reliability and comparability of ESG ratings, helping build confidence in the information investors rely on. The regime applies to firms or organisations providing ESG ratings and assessments to ensure reliability across the market. The FCA has published guidance to help firms understand whether they may be in scope. Laura Dawes, director of authorisations and sustainable finance at the FCA, said: 'Trusted information is essential for well-functioning markets. These rules will help improve transparency and raise standards across the ESG ratings market while supporting competition, innovation and growth. 'Firms should check now whether they are in scope and start preparing for authorisation. We'll continue to provide practical support to help them prepare.'The new framework introduces requirements covering transparency, governance, systems and controls, the management of conflicts of interest, and engagement with users of ESG ratings and rated entities. It is designed to be proportionate to firms' size and activities and is informed by international and existing standards. Firms that may be in scope should start preparing now. ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. The FCA will provide webinars and access to its Pre-Application Support Service to help firms prepare. Firms should now: understand whether the framework could apply to their activities review the final rules and guidanceconsider whether they need FCA authorisationstart preparing for implementationengage early with FCA support servicesNotes to editorsRead the FCA’s Policy Statement and final rules, PS26/22, ‘ESG ratings: final regime’.The new framework takes effect on 29 June 2028. From that date, firms providing ESG ratings in the UK will need FCA authorisation and to have the relevant permission before carrying on that activity, unless an exemption applies.ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. We are staggering application periods and encourage firms to apply as early as possible within their window. ESG ratings generally assess how companies or other entities, assets, or financial products perform against environmental, social and governance criteria. They are used by asset managers, lenders, benchmark administrators and others to inform capital allocation decisions and manage risk, among other uses. The approach is shaped by international standards, including recommendations from the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO). The final rules follow the FCA’s consultation, CP25/34, which opened on 1 December 2025 and closed on 31 March 2026. The regulatory framework follows government legislation bringing the provision of ESG ratings within the FCA’s remit in October 2025. 95% of respondents to the government’s consultation supported the move. The regime regulates how ESG ratings are produced, governed and communicated. It does not prescribe a particular sustainability view or methodology. There is strong investor demand for ESG information. The FCA's Financial Lives Survey 2024 found 72% of adults with investments or a defined contribution pension wanted their investments to do some good as well as provide a financial return.

title: FCA sets expectations for firms making car finance settlement offers
raw_summary: Research shows consumers want the choice, rather than wait for the legal challenges to conclude. Almost 9 out of 10 (89%) car finance customers who have complained or are considering doing so want the choice of an offer of compensation now, rather than waiting for the legal challenges to the FCA's compensation scheme to conclude. 86% would be comfortable making the decision, and 61% say they’d accept an offer in line with the scheme. Timing matters for many: 77% say receiving compensation sooner would make a great deal or fair amount of difference to their financial situation.The survey findings are being released today alongside the FCA's expectations for lenders who want to make settlement offers to those owed compensation under its scheme, while legal challenges continue. This comes as Barclays Partner Finance confirms it will make settlement offers to some of its customers owed compensation.The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme.Lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes that they will keep any money received, even if the outcome of the legal challenges means they would have received less. However, they also wouldn’t be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge means they would have been paid more. As consumers can reject an offer and leave their claim to be dealt with under the scheme, these offers can’t be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service for review.Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:'Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.'Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.'To help consumers make informed decisions, the FCA has published a factsheet (PDF) that lenders must share with customers when making settlement offers. Not all lenders are likely to make offers, and those that do may only make them to some customers owed compensation. The FCA will regularly update its website with lenders making settlement offers to help consumers check whether an offer is genuine. Firms are expected to notify the FCA if they plan to make offers.Payouts under the motor finance compensation scheme were due to start this year. The scheme is currently partially suspended, pending the outcome of legal challenges due to be heard between 16 February and 3 March 2027. Under the partial suspension, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and continue progressing complaints as far as possible, but do not need to calculate or pay compensation under the scheme until the legal process concludes.Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained should complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free. There is no need to use a law firm or claims management company, which may charge up to 36% of any compensation, including VAT.Notes to editorsResearch conducted by Kantar, surveying 1,000 motor finance customers online between 25 and 28 June 2026. Findings cited are based on a subset of 590 respondents who said they had made or were considering making a motor finance complaint.Barclays press release.Statement confirming motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027.Statement on the partial suspension of the motor finance scheme and what it means for firms and consumers.

title: Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
raw_summary: We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

title: FCA publishes terms of reference for independent review concerning Mr Andriesz
raw_summary: We have published the terms of reference for the review into our handling of interactions with Mr Simon Andriesz, a whistleblower who made protected disclosures to the FCA. We shared our condolences following Mr Andriesz's tragic death and our thoughts remain with his family and loved ones.The review was commissioned by our non-executive directors. It is being conducted by Lea Paterson CBE, an independent non-executive director of the FCA.When we announced the review, we said it would examine how we interacted with Mr Andriesz. The review will now also look at whether we met our responsibilities under whistleblowing law and followed our own policies and procedures when handling his whistleblowing reports, including his concerns that he had experienced detriment. It will cover the period from at least 2017 to 2026.The review will identify any lessons learned and make recommendations for improvements to our future engagement with external whistleblowers and vulnerable individuals.We previously said we aimed to publish findings in early 2027. Given this broader scope and the need to examine evidence spanning many years, more time is needed to complete the review thoroughly.A progress update will be published in January 2027, with the final report expected in spring 2027.Read the terms of reference (PDF).

title: b12550: ggml : add backend scheduler tests (#27258)
raw_summary: Adds initial scheduler stress tests Adds new sleep op to simplify scheduler testing Adds testcase addressing #23321 Adds experimental vulkan GGML_OP_SLEEP Improves structure and naming of previous tests. Adds new tests, including one which detects the nkvo-bug correctly, and validates the proposed hotfix. Cleanup: Removes CUDA specific comments and nvtx-markers Fix: forgot to add sleep specific test case Fix oversights identified by CI Drops default prints so that it behaves like other ctests. Adds -v flag to toggle this behavior Fix: Early exit in CPU-only settings (cause for graviton CI fails) Improves stress_test_linked_list by removing overlap with test_chain_all_backends and test_pair_user_inputs. The latter ones test either activations or user inputs in isolation and just once, whereas the stress test tests all combinations multiple rounds Exclude ACCEL devices from new tests due to incompatibility Fixes vulkan test failure in llvmpipe Adds asserts, improves comments and some checks Fixes nitpicks in white-space and variable naming Adds comments that certain vk drivers could time OP_SLEEP incorrectly Drops limitiation to CPU/GPU in test-sleep Aligns OP_SLEEP guards in cuda with vk guards (input shape and contiguity) Implements feedback for OP_SLEEP to work in place (no copy) Apply non-code suggestions from JohannesGaesslers code review Co-authored-by: Johannes Gäßler johannesg@5d6.de Removes struct backend_supports; enables tests to return skip, instead of only pass/fail Make clang-tidy happy Removes sched_backend_caps, improves create_test_scheduler according to feedback (L149) Removes "name" field from struct sched_check in favor of ggml_set_name/ggml_get_name Drops unnecessary shader_clock.comp test and guards Replaces sched_ prefixes with helper_ prefix Moves test suite to new RAII types for better memory management Adds sleep option to test_chain_all_backends Adds sleep option to first-run arm of the y-shaped test Fix switchcase order for legibility in stress_test_dag Simplfies stress_test_linked_list via double for-loop Adds pseudo-random input to stress_test_linked_list, and runs all transitions both with and without CPU input (next to activation copy as input) Fix RPC Proto patch due to GGML_OPS bump Adds ggml-cpp.h treatment to test-sleep.cpp Adds TODO pointers for subsequent additional tests. Apply suggestion to ggml.h Co-authored-by: Johannes Gäßler johannesg@5d6.de Apply suggestion to tests/test-backend-sched.cpp Co-authored-by: Johannes Gäßler johannesg@5d6.de Apply suggestion to tests/test-backend-sched.cpp Co-authored-by: Johannes Gäßler johannesg@5d6.de Fixes node compatibility check to not take buffer locations into account. This led to skipped tests due to incorrectly rejected ops due to wrong buffer locations in multi-GPU (which is one of the scheduler behaviors under test) Apply batched suggestions from gg code review Co-authored-by: Georgi Gerganov ggerganov@gmail.com Completes callsite change of gg-suggestion Switch test-sleep from std::chrono::steady_clock::now() to ggml_time_us to avoid mac clock drift and spurious test failures. This makes the test a bit nonsensical on CPU (same clock checks itself), but the test still has merit on the other backends where independent device clocks are used. title: b12549
raw_summary: llama: fixes for Inkling 2 attention mask ( #32429 ) llama : give Inkling2 its own relative-position attention input The Inkling2 graph built its flash attention mask from the hybrid iswa input and passed it to build_attn through a new kq_mask argument. That argument let a caller pair its own dense mask with the kv_rows of llm_graph_input_attn_kv_iswa, whose mask follows the per-sequence cell lists whenever kv_rows is enabled. Add llm_graph_input_attn_rel_pos instead. It owns dense KQ masks and the query-to-cell distances, fills both from the same cells, and its build_attn overload adds the per-head bias to its own mask and never passes kv_rows. The iswa build_attn is back to its previous signature; its body moves to build_attn_iswa_impl, which both overloads call. Inkling2 now folds the per-query sink into the bias with and without flash attention, so build_attn_mha no longer needs the per-query sink path. Assisted-By: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com inkling2 : make the expert weight scale and final logit softcap optional Load both keys as optional and skip them when they are zero, as other models do, instead of rejecting zero at load. Assisted-By: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com llama : build kv_rows masks for the hybrid iswa memory llm_graph_input_mem_hybrid_iswa checked its masks with can_reuse_attn_mask, which expects kv_rows whenever they are enabled, but built them dense. With a unified cache and flash attention the check always failed, and hybrid iswa models (LFM2, LFM3, Inkling2) never reused a graph. Build the masks with build_attn_inp_attn_mask, like the plain iswa input. Assisted-By: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com llama : make the relative-position input a hybrid iswa input Address review: llm_graph_input_mem_hybrid_iswa_rel derives from llm_graph_input_mem_hybrid_iswa and owns the attention and recurrent inputs, so Inkling2 builds one memory input instead of two. Its attention input is built with dense masks, can_reuse checks them as dense, and its build_attn asserts that the mask has no kv_rows (TODO: a kv_rows variant). build_attn_iswa_impl is now a static helper. Assisted-By: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com llama : compose the hybrid iswa rel input, format inkling2 Address review: llm_graph_input_mem_hybrid_iswa_rel owns its attention and recurrent inputs like the other composite inputs instead of deriving from llm_graph_input_mem_hybrid_iswa. Format src/models/inkling2.cpp like the other model sources: grouped and aligned key and tensor loading, descriptive per-layer names, blank lines and section comments between the steps, and cb() names for the intermediate tensors. The graph is unchanged. title: b12543
raw_summary: metal : CONV_2D tensor API for M5, split-K for all chips ( #32542 ) metal: add a tensor API conv_2d kernel and split long reductions The conv_2d matmul kernel runs on simdgroup matrices only, and gives each threadgroup the whole reduction of its output tile. On M5 this leaves the tensor cores unused, and convolutions with few output positions and a long reduction (IC * KW * KH in the thousands) run a handful of threadgroups on an otherwise idle GPU. Add kernel_conv_2d_mm_tensor for devices with the tensor API: like kernel_mul_mm, it gathers the patches of 64 output positions into threadgroup memory as the left operand and reads the kernel rows from device memory as the right operand. Devices without the tensor API keep the simdgroup kernel. Both kernels can now split the reduction until there are enough threadgroups: each split writes its partial sums to a buffer placed after the output, as flash attention does, and a small kernel adds them in a fixed order, so the result stays deterministic. CONV_2D is marked as an op whose allocation may exceed its output size. test-backend-ops -o CONV_2D passes, with and without GGML_METAL_TENSOR_DISABLE. CONV_2D, F16 kernel, us/run on an M5 Max: [19,19,256,16] k [4,4,256,4096] 19008 -> 5235 [16,16,128,8] k [3,3,128,512] 333 -> 124 [1536,1536,32,1] k [3,3,32,64] 12086 -> 6512 [33,1,1280,1] k [3,1,1280,1280] s2 659 -> 33 [2054,1,768,1] k [7,1,768,768] 3161 -> 699 metal: walk the conv_2d patches incrementally, size splits by output The patch gather of both conv_2d matmul kernels spent most of its time on address math: 64-bit multiplies, divisions and four bound checks per value. Walk the reduction index with 32-bit byte offsets inside the image, updated by additions, with one unsigned compare per bound; the host checks that an image fits. The tensor kernel no longer gathers the reduction indices past the end of its split. The number of splits now targets about 1M partial sums, with at least 3 reduction steps per split, instead of counting the tiles of one kernel. CONV_2D, F16 kernel, us/run on an M5 Max: [19,19,256,16] k [4,4,256,4096] 4998 -> 4512 [1536,1536,32,1] k [3,3,32,64] 6721 -> 5354 [4096,1,1024,1] k [7,1,1024,1024] 2701 -> 2236 [2054,1,768,1] k [7,1,768,768] 1050 -> 871 with GGML_METAL_TENSOR_DISABLE: [4096,1,1024,1] k [7,1,1024,1024] 9047 -> 8283 nit: share the CONV_2D simdgroup count between host and kernel kernel_conv_2d_mm and its pipeline both hardcoded 4 simdgroups per threadgroup. N_SG_CONV_2D in ggml-metal-impl.h now feeds the kernel constant and res.nsg, so the dispatch and the kernel cannot drift apart. metal: fall back to the generic conv_2d kernel for images past 4 GiB The matmul conv_2d kernels walk the patches with 32-bit byte offsets inside an image. title: v2.9.0
raw_summary: Features api: add source and error codes to the RBAC Role read endpoints api: add Update Bundle, which sets a Claude Tag Bundle's instructions, and return instructions on Bundle Bug Fixes credentials: write the credentials file on Windows with Python 3.12 and earlier tools: compare directory names exactly when confining file tool and upload paths on Windows tools: fully resolve file tool paths that pass through a dangling symlink tools: ignore ripgrep config files in the agent toolset's grep tool tools: keep an existing skill directory when the download or extraction that would replace it fails tools: keep the session tool runner's max_idle countdown running when a session thread terminates If the runner fails to read the session's event history after a reconnect, a termination that then arrives on the event stream still cancels the countdown, until the next idle or successful read. tools: leave symlinks that point outside /memories out of listings tools: look for ripgrep only in absolute PATH entries in the agent toolset's grep tool The tool no longer runs an rg from a relative or empty PATH entry or, on Windows, from the current directory. On Windows it looks for rg.exe , so an rg.cmd , rg.bat or rg.com is no longer used. With no other rg on PATH , the tool uses its built-in search. tools: pass over an rg inside the directories the agent toolset's file tools can write grep passes over an rg that resolves to somewhere inside workdir or allowed_roots , whatever the letter case of the names. It uses the next rg on PATH , or the built-in search when there is none. With a workdir that holds every rg on the host, such as / , every search is a built-in search. rg no longer gets the ANTHROPIC_* variables of the process, like the shell of bash . tools: read memory files only through the path that was validated tools: read only regular files in the grep tool's built-in search The built-in search of grep passes over a FIFO or a device in the directory it walks, as ripgrep does. Reading one could block the search, and the event loop with it, forever. tools: stop EnvironmentWorker from running tools for a terminated session For a terminated session, the worker now force-stops the work item right after it retrieves the session, before it downloads skills or memory stores. It no longer raises SessionMemoryError for such a session. The API reports an archived session as terminated . tools: stop the grep tool after 30 seconds of CPU time when ripgrep is not installed tools: stop the session tool runner from running the tool calls of a terminated session thread The runner also no longer yields these calls, including a denied call ( confirmation="deny" ) and a call to a tool that it does not own. The one exception is a call whose tool is already running when the thread terminates: the runner yields it with posted=False and posts no result. Chores api: deprecate old beta header values The API still accepts these values, but a later release removes them from the SDKs. Delete prompt-caching-2024-07-31 , pdfs-2024-09-25 , token-counting-2024-11-01 , token-efficient-tools-2025-02-19 , extended-cache-ttl-2025-04-11 , cache-diagnosis-2026-04-07 and ce-user-management-2026-07-13 from your requests. files-api-2025-04-14 and skills-2025-10-02 select the beta response shapes, so follow the Files API and Skills migration guides before you delete them. In C#, the AnthropicBeta enum's members have new numbers, so code compiled against an earlier SDK version sends a different beta value, with no error, until you rebuild it. api: stop sending an old beta header on batch requests beta.messages.batches no longer sends message-batches-2024-09-24 , which the API doesn't need. If your client sets a default anthropic-beta header, these requests now send it, where in some SDKs the old value replaced it. The API still accepts the old value. If you set it yourself, delete it: a later release removes it from the SDKs. docs: add an example value for the workspace name docs: clarify when the auto permission policy denies a tool call docs: clarify which workspaces an external key can be attached to docs: recommend multiagent_20261001 over the coordinator type docs: say when organization_id is required on plugin reads tests: let idle test workers take queued tests

title: Towards a Science of Capable Autonomous Agents & Provable Safety — Part II
raw_summary: Part II: Provable Safety In Part I, I talked about what agents must contain as they become increasingly capable. Here, I talk about having provable guarantees on their safety, in spite of these capabilities. This is in large part a contrast from what AI safety used to be like, where more capability ensured more safety: e.g. if a self-driving car can’t reliably detect objects, it’s obviously unsafe. Instead, what we are talking about is: how do we ensure capable systems remain open to human correction, even when it’s otherwise suboptimal for completing the task?  Suppose an agent is editing a document when a notification announces that its computer will shut down. It knows this will prevent it from finishing, and it knows how to cancel the shutdown. If the priority is completing the document, the next step seems obvious. We would welcome this resourcefulness if the obstacle were a broken application. We would be less pleased if it were our request for the agent to stop. An agent that bypasses an obstacle may also bypass a stop request. In fact, the same predictive knowledge that helps an agent finish a task can help it work around an intervention. In these […]
